Preferred chezmoi workflow — edit the target, not the source name: run chezmoi edit with a destination path (for example chezmoi edit ~/.zshrc). chezmoi opens your $EDITOR on the file in its target location (by default via a hardlink when possible), so the buffer path looks like .zshrc or .config/foo/bar and normal editor filetype detection applies. The design FAQ states explicitly that chezmoi edit arguments are target paths so you do not have to reason about dot_ prefixes while editing and syntax highlighting works.

Why source-tree names are awkward: in the chezmoi source state, paths use filename metadata (dot_bashrc, private_config, executable_, templates as *.tmpl, and so on). Those names are not the final dotfile paths, so an editor opening dot_zshrc in the repo often picks the wrong language. That is expected; chezmoi’s accepted mitigation is chezmoi edit, not a special highlighter built into chezmoi itself.

Editing directly in the source directory: chezmoi does not ship editor integrations for every editor. For Vim/Neovim, the Editor user guide documents alker0/chezmoi.vim, which maps dot_* names to real paths for filetype detection and, for *.tmpl, layers go-template highlighting on top of the underlying language. The same guide lists Lilja/vim-chezmoi (apply on save with chezmoi edit) and xvzc/chezmoi.nvim. For Emacs, chezmoi.el is the documented option.

Vim modeline in the source file: if you insist on editing dot_* files in the repo without a plugin, the design FAQ also recommends a Vim modeline at the top of the source file (for example # vim: filetype=zsh in dot_zshrc). That is a Vim convention chezmoi documents, not a chezmoi parser feature.

Templates: plain chezmoi edit gives correct highlighting for non-template targets. For *.tmpl in the source tree, use chezmoi.vim (or similar) so you get both the base language and template syntax; some dotfiles repos also add modelines such as vim:ft=toml.gotexttmpl in template headers as a local convention.

VS Code / GUI editors: configure edit.command / edit.args in ~/.config/chezmoi/chezmoi.toml (for Code, include --wait so chezmoi does not return early — see the Editor guide). Use chezmoi edit for highlighting via real target paths; for raw source-tree editing in VS Code you rely on language-specific extensions or files.associations, not a first-party chezmoi VS Code extension in the official docs.

Scripts are files in the chezmoi/Source/Directory whose names begin with run_. They are executed by chezmoi apply in alphabetical order.
chezmoi/Script/run_onchange_ — executes only when the script's rendered content has changed since the last successful run
chezmoi/Script/run_once_ — executes once per unique rendered-content SHA256; will not re-run unless the content itself changes
By default scripts run during the target-state update pass, interleaved alphabetically with file updates.
Add before_ to run before any target files are updated: e.g. run_once_before_install-password-manager.sh
Add after_ to run after all target files are updated: e.g. run_onchange_after_reload-config.sh
Modifiers combine freely with any script type.
Place scripts in .chezmoiscripts/ at the source root so they execute as normal scripts without creating a directory in the chezmoi/Target/State.
Add a .tmpl suffix to use chezmoi/Template variables. If the rendered output is empty or whitespace-only, the script is skipped — useful for OS-gating scripts.
Scripts must include a #! shebang line. No need to set the executable bit manually.
All scripts must be idempotent, including run_onchange_ and run_once_ variants.
A numeric ordering prefix (e.g. 75-) controls execution order when alphabetical order alone is insufficient.
In dry-run mode (--dry-run), scripts are not executed.
(the [hooks] section in chezmoi.toml) is a separate mechanism: hook commands run before/after lifecycle events and always execute, even in dry-run mode.
A script whose filename begins with run_ (without once_ or onchange_) executes every time chezmoi apply is run.
Use sparingly; prefer chezmoi/Script/run_onchange_ or chezmoi/Script/run_once_ to avoid unnecessary re-execution.
Must be idempotent — chezmoi makes no attempt to prevent duplicate side-effects.
See chezmoi/Script for naming conventions, timing modifiers, and the .chezmoiscripts/ directory.

A script prefixed run_once_ executes once per unique rendered-content version. chezmoi stores the SHA256 hash of each run in its state database; a script with previously-seen content is silently skipped, even if the filename changes.
To force a re-run, clear the recorded state: chezmoi state delete-bucket --bucket=scriptState

For chezmoi/Template scripts, the content is hashed after template execution, so changing template data (e.g. .chezmoidata) that alters the rendered output counts as new content and triggers a re-run.
run_once_before_ — runs before chezmoi updates target files; common for bootstrapping (e.g. installing a password manager before reading secrets)
run_once_after_ — runs after chezmoi updates target files
run_once_ is appropriate for one-time setup where re-running on every content change is undesirable.
If you want automatic re-execution whenever a plugin list or config file changes, use chezmoi/Script/run_onchange_ instead.
See chezmoi/Script for full naming conventions and the .chezmoiscripts/ directory.
A script prefixed run_onchange_ re-executes only when its rendered content has changed since the last successful run. chezmoi tracks the SHA256 hash of the rendered script body.

This is the canonical yazi plugin management pattern: when package.toml changes, chezmoi recomputes the hash, detects the script content has changed, and re-runs ya pkg install.
Scripts execute alphabetically by filename. A numeric prefix (e.g. run_onchange_after_75-install-yazi-packages.sh.tmpl) controls position relative to other scripts.

Chronological order arranges items by when they happened — earlier before later — so the sequence itself is the index.
Journals, logs, and feeds use it so a reader can ask what happened next?

In this garden, journaling is deliberately chronological; knowledge gardening is not. Related pages should sit near each other the way a Graph/Database clusters neighbors, not in the order they were filed.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Alpha/Bet/ic/al/Order — by letters of the alphabet, for human-readable lists of words.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Lexicographic/Order — by the full character repertoire of a name, including digits and punctuation; the order s actually use.
Other orders in the garden answer different questions:
Time is the key — the sort key is a date or timestamp, not a title.
Precision follows knowledge — year, month, or day per Logseq/Date; do not fake a day when only a year is known.
Sequence is not proximity — two notes written on consecutive days may be about unrelated things; chronology does not cluster by topic.
A journal page journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md and a wikilink in the YYYY-MM-DD Day shape are chronological addresses.
Entity paths that embed <YY>/<MM> (blogs, podcasts, books) use chronology as a secondary key after creator and type, so works still cluster by who made them.
A blog post path Person/<Name>/Blog/<YY>/<MM>/<slug> — dated, but nested under the author.
A series path that also uses an ordinal — publication year and reading order can diverge; Logseq/Entity/Series prefers the ordinal when the published sequence numbers its parts.
"Filing by date keeps related things together" — False unless the relatedness is the date (a trip, a conference). Topic clusters need a graph-like layout instead.
"Alphabetical and chronological are the two orders" — Incomplete; filesystem sort is Lexicographic/Order, which is a generalization of Alpha/Bet/ic/al/Order and is not a time order.

In biology, a clade is a group made up of one common ancestor and all of its descendants. Biologists also call it a monophyletic group.
From Ancient Greek kládos, "shoot, branch". The biologist Julian Huxley coined the word in 1957, in the Nature paper "The Three Types of Evolutionary Process".
Clades nest inside one another, because each branch of the tree of life splits into smaller branches.

A group that leaves out some descendants of its common ancestor is paraphyletic. The traditional class Reptilia is the usual example: it holds the last common ancestor of reptiles and its descendants, except the birds.
Clades are the basic unit of cladistics, the approach to taxonomy that most fields of biology now use.

In the entity system described on Logseq/Entity, the clade of Logseq/Entity/Person would be Person together with every entity that is a kind of person, such as Logseq/Entity/Person/Maker/Music and Logseq/Entity/Person/Knowledge Gardener. In Logseq/Entity/Hierarchy/Discussion/Analysis/Opus/26/10/01/0611 ET Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage, Claude Opus recommends lineage for the chain that runs the other way, from Musician up to Person.
